enthalpy-of-reaction-s1.title: Four thermochemical equations
enthalpy-of-reaction-s1.text: Each ΔH is for the reaction exactly as written, in kJ per mole of reaction, at 25 °C and 1 atm.

enthalpy-of-reaction-s2.title: An iron hand warmer
enthalpy-of-reaction-s2.text:
A disposable hand warmer holds iron powder, salt water and charcoal in a pouch that lets air in. When the pouch is opened, the iron reacts with oxygen from the air:

4 Fe(s) + 3 O₂(g) → 2 Fe₂O₃(s)    ΔH = −1648.4 kJ/mol

Molar mass of Fe: 55.85 g/mol.

items.q: Using Equation A, what is q for the reacting system, in kJ, when 11.0 g of propane, C₃H₈ (44.10 g/mol), burns completely?

mistakes.why: Sign: burning releases energy, so q for the reacting system is negative.
Value: you multiplied grams by kJ per mole. Convert grams of propane to moles first.
Value: you divided by the 5 of O₂. Propane has a coefficient of 1, so moles of propane = moles of reaction.

why.correct: n(C₃H₈) = 11.0 g ÷ 44.10 g/mol = 0.2494 mol. One mole of reaction burns 1 mol of C₃H₈, so q = 0.2494 mol × (−2220 kJ/mol) = −553.7 → −554 kJ (three significant figures, from 11.0 g). Negative: the system releases energy.

items.q: Using Equation B, what is the enthalpy change, in kJ, for forming 1.00 mol of NH₃(g) from N₂ and H₂?

mistakes.why: Value: −92.2 kJ is for 2 mol of NH₃, as the equation is written. Scale to 1.00 mol: divide by 2.
Value: you doubled instead of halving. The equation already makes 2 mol of NH₃.

why.correct: Equation B makes 2 mol of NH₃ for −92.2 kJ. For 1.00 mol, halve it: 1.00 mol NH₃ × (−92.2 kJ / 2 mol NH₃) = −46.1 kJ.

items.q: What is ΔH for the reaction 2 NH₃(g) → N₂(g) + 3 H₂(g)?
options: −92.2 kJ/mol
+46.1 kJ/mol
+92.2 kJ/mol
−184.4 kJ/mol

why.correct: Reversing a thermochemical equation changes the sign of ΔH and keeps its size: +92.2 kJ/mol.
options: Reversing a reaction flips the sign of ΔH: decomposing ammonia absorbs what forming it released.
The coefficients match Equation B exactly (2 NH₃), so the size stays 92.2 kJ.
Right: this is Equation B reversed, so ΔH has the same size and the opposite sign.
Nothing is doubled here, and the sign must flip on reversing.

items.q: Using Equation D, how much energy, in kJ, must be absorbed to decompose 50.0 g of CaCO₃ (100.09 g/mol)?

mistakes.why: Value: convert the 50.0 g of CaCO₃ to moles before multiplying by kJ per mole.
Sign: Equation D has a positive ΔH, so decomposing CaCO₃ absorbs energy; the amount absorbed is positive.

items.q: Using Equation C, how much energy, in kJ, is absorbed when enough HgO decomposes to make 4.00 g of O₂ (32.00 g/mol)?

mistakes.why: Value: you counted 2 mol of reaction per mole of O₂. Equation C makes 1 mol of O₂ per mole of reaction (the 2 belongs to HgO and Hg).
Value: you halved the energy. The 181.6 kJ goes with 1 mol of O₂ formed, so use it directly.

why.correct: n(O₂) = 4.00 g ÷ 32.00 g/mol = 0.125 mol. One mole of reaction makes 1 mol of O₂ and absorbs 181.6 kJ, so q = 0.125 mol × 181.6 kJ/mol = 22.7 kJ absorbed.

items.q: How much energy, in kJ, is released when 5.00 g of iron reacts completely?

mistakes.why: Value: −1648.4 kJ goes with 4 mol of Fe. Divide by 4 to get the energy per mole of iron.
Value: you used the 2 of Fe₂O₃. The question gives iron, so use iron's coefficient, 4.

why.correct: n(Fe) = 5.00 g ÷ 55.85 g/mol = 0.08953 mol. The equation releases 1648.4 kJ per 4 mol of Fe: 0.08953 mol Fe × (1648.4 kJ / 4 mol Fe) = 36.89 → 36.9 kJ released.

items.q: A pouch holds 10.0 g of iron, but only 0.0500 mol of O₂ reaches the iron before the pouch is sealed again. How much energy, in kJ, is released?

mistakes.why: Value: you used all the iron. O₂ runs out first (10.0 g Fe needs 0.134 mol O₂), so base the energy on the 0.0500 mol of O₂.
Value: −1648.4 kJ goes with 3 mol of O₂. Divide by 3 to get the energy per mole of O₂.

why.correct: Iron: 0.1791 mol would need 0.1343 mol O₂, more than the 0.0500 mol available, so O₂ is limiting. Energy = 0.0500 mol O₂ × (1648.4 kJ / 3 mol O₂) = 27.47 → 27.5 kJ.

items.q: Your hands are the surroundings of the hand-warmer reaction. Which statement about q is correct?
options: q for the reaction is positive and q for your hands is negative.
q for the reaction and q for your hands are both negative.
q for the reaction is negative and q for your hands is zero.
q for the reaction is negative and q for your hands is positive.

why.correct: q(surroundings) = −q(reaction). The reaction's ΔH is negative, so the surroundings gain energy.
options: That would describe an endothermic reaction, like a cold pack.
Energy lost by one is gained by the other, so the signs are opposite.
Your hands warm up, so they gain energy: their q is positive.
Right: the reaction releases energy and your hands absorb it.

items.q: Which thermochemical equation is equivalent to the hand-warmer equation?
options: 2 Fe(s) + 3/2 O₂(g) → Fe₂O₃(s), ΔH = −824.2 kJ/mol
2 Fe(s) + 3/2 O₂(g) → Fe₂O₃(s), ΔH = −1648.4 kJ/mol
2 Fe₂O₃(s) → 4 Fe(s) + 3 O₂(g), ΔH = −1648.4 kJ/mol
8 Fe(s) + 6 O₂(g) → 4 Fe₂O₃(s), ΔH = −824.2 kJ/mol

why.correct: ΔH scales with the coefficients: halve the equation, halve ΔH; reverse it, flip the sign.
options: Right: every coefficient is halved, so ΔH is halved too.
The coefficients were halved but ΔH was not; ΔH must be scaled the same way.
Reversed, so the sign of ΔH must change to +1648.4 kJ/mol.
Doubling the coefficients doubles ΔH, to −3296.8 kJ/mol.

items.q: A thermochemical equation is written with ΔH = −92.2 kJ/mol. What does "per mole" refer to?
options: One mole of each substance in the equation
One mole of reaction: the amounts given by the coefficients as written
One mole of the first reactant listed
One mole of atoms in the products

why.correct: "kJ/mol" in a thermochemical equation means per mole of reaction, the reaction occurring once in the mole amounts given by the coefficients.
options: The coefficients differ (1, 3, 2), so "per mole of each" would give different answers.
Right: ΔH is for the whole equation as written, here 1 mol N₂ + 3 mol H₂ → 2 mol NH₃.
The first reactant is one choice, but the value is tied to every coefficient together.
ΔH is not counted per mole of atoms.

items.q: Methane burns as CH₄(g) + 2 O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2 H₂O(l), ΔH = −890.3 kJ/mol. Vaporizing water at 25 °C absorbs 44.0 kJ/mol. What is ΔH when the water is formed as a gas instead?
options: −978.3 kJ/mol
−846.3 kJ/mol
−802.3 kJ/mol
−890.3 kJ/mol

why.correct: Forming 2 H₂O(g) instead of 2 H₂O(l) skips condensing 2 mol of water, which would release 88.0 kJ. ΔH = −890.3 + 88.0 = −802.3 kJ/mol.
options: Gaseous water sits higher in enthalpy than liquid water, so less energy is released, not more.
Two moles of water form, so the correction is 2 × 44.0 kJ, not 44.0 kJ.
Right: the gaseous water is 2 × 44.0 = 88.0 kJ higher in enthalpy, so less energy is released: −890.3 + 88.0.
The state of the products matters: making a gas instead of a liquid keeps 88.0 kJ in the products.

items.q: Using CH₄(g) + 2 O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2 H₂O(l), ΔH = −890.3 kJ/mol, what mass of methane (16.04 g/mol), in g, must burn to release 1.00 × 10³ kJ?

mistakes.why: Value: that is the amount in moles. Multiply by the molar mass, 16.04 g/mol, for grams.
Value: you divided the wrong way. Moles = energy needed ÷ energy per mole.

items.q: The reaction 2 SO₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2 SO₃(g) has ΔH = −197.8 kJ/mol. Which statements are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Forming 1 mol of SO₃ releases 98.9 kJ.
For SO₃(g) → SO₂(g) + ½ O₂(g), ΔH = +98.9 kJ/mol.
For 4 SO₂(g) + 2 O₂(g) → 4 SO₃(g), ΔH = −197.8 kJ/mol.
Reacting 2 mol of SO₂ with 3 mol of O₂ releases 593.4 kJ.
The reaction absorbs 197.8 kJ for each 2 mol of SO₃ formed.
Forming 0.500 mol of SO₃ releases 49.5 kJ.

why.correct: Scale ΔH with the coefficients, flip its sign on reversing, and base the energy on the amount that actually reacts.
options: The equation forms 2 mol of SO₃ for 197.8 kJ, so 1 mol releases half: 98.9 kJ.
Halved and reversed: half the size, opposite sign.
Doubling the coefficients doubles ΔH, to −395.6 kJ/mol.
O₂ is in excess; 2 mol of SO₂ reacts with just 1 mol of O₂, releasing 197.8 kJ.
A negative ΔH means energy is released, not absorbed.
0.500 mol SO₃ × (197.8 kJ / 2 mol SO₃) = 49.45 kJ, which is 49.5 kJ.

items.q: The decomposition 2 KClO₃(s) → 2 KCl(s) + 3 O₂(g) has ΔH = −78.0 kJ/mol. A student decomposes twice as much KClO₃ as before. Predict how each value compares with the first run.

variables.name: Energy released
variables.why: Twice the moles react, so twice the energy is released.

variables.name: ΔH for the equation as written
variables.why: ΔH belongs to the equation, per mole of reaction; it does not depend on how much is used.

variables.name: Moles of O₂ produced per mole of KClO₃
variables.why: The ratio is set by the coefficients, 3 : 2.

why.correct: The energy of a run scales with the amount; ΔH per mole of reaction and mole ratios do not.

items.q: Photosynthesis, 6 CO₂(g) + 6 H₂O(l) → C₆H₁₂O₆(s) + 6 O₂(g), has ΔH = +2802.5 kJ/mol. What is ΔH for the overall reaction of cellular respiration, C₆H₁₂O₆(s) + 6 O₂(g) → 6 CO₂(g) + 6 H₂O(l)?
options: −467.1 kJ/mol
0 kJ/mol, because the two reactions cancel

why.correct: Reversing a thermochemical equation changes the sign of ΔH: respiration releases 2802.5 kJ per mole of glucose.
options: Reversing an equation flips the sign of ΔH: respiration releases what photosynthesis absorbs.
That is 2802.5 ÷ 6. The coefficients are the same in both equations, so the size is unchanged.
Right: respiration is photosynthesis written in reverse, so ΔH flips sign.
Each reaction has its own ΔH; they cancel only when added together.

items.q: Cellular respiration releases 2802.5 kJ per mole of glucose (180.16 g/mol). How much energy, in kJ, is released per gram of glucose?

mistakes.why: Value: you multiplied. kJ/mol ÷ g/mol = kJ/g.
Value: that is grams per kJ. Divide the energy per mole by the mass per mole.

items.q: In an open vessel at constant pressure, N₂(g) + 3 H₂(g) → 2 NH₃(g), ΔH = −92.2 kJ/mol, runs once as written. What is q for the surroundings?
options: 0 kJ, because the energy stays in the reacting gases
Right: the reaction releases 92.2 kJ and the surroundings absorb it.
That is q for the reaction. The surroundings have the opposite sign.
The reaction runs once as written, making 2 mol of NH₃, so all 92.2 kJ is transferred.
Energy crosses the boundary between the reacting gases and everything around them, so the surroundings warm.
